title: Rook against pawn
summary: The cut-off, counting tempi, the shoulder and the defence that promotes to a knight.
part.cutting.title: Cut off or get behind
part.cutting.summary: The rook cuts off the black king or gets behind the pawn while the king comes.
part.counting.title: Count and shoulder
part.counting.summary: One tempo decides everything: count the moves and shoulder the black king away.
part.around.title: Going around and gaining time
part.around.summary: When the black king blocks the way: going round in front of the pawn and the check that gains time.
part.knightTrap.title: Promoting to a knight
part.knightTrap.summary: The resource that saves the pawn, and how not to fall for it.
part.saavedraEnd.title: Saavedra and summary
part.saavedraEnd.summary: When the pawn beats the rook, the three rules and the ending against the machine.
step.t_cut: The pawn is racing to promote and your king is far away. How can the rook gain the time your king needs to arrive?
step.t_cut.hint1: Look for a rank where the rook stands between the black king and the pawn's path.
step.intro: Rook against pawn looks easy: a rook is worth far more than a pawn. But the pawn walks on its own, and the rook needs its king to win. So this ending is a race: if your king arrives in time, the rook wins; if it arrives late, the pawn queens or costs the rook, and it is a draw. Before you move, ask three questions. Can I cut the black king off with the rook? How many moves does my king need to reach the pawn? And is the black king in front of the pawn or behind it? Here the black king is still far from d1, and the rook can separate it from the pawn.
step.cut: Cut the black king off. The rook on a rank between the king and the pawn's path leaves the pawn alone, and a lone pawn is food for the rook. Then bring your king.
step.cut.hint: Ra5: the fifth rank is now off limits for the black king. Then Kg6.
step.cut.done: The black king cannot cross the fifth rank. If the pawn runs, the rook catches it; if the black king walks around, your king is already there. Cutting off is the first tool: it costs one move and gains several.
step.behindIdea: When you cannot cut the king off, put the rook behind the pawn. It stops the pawn from moving without an escort: at every step, the black king has to stand next to it to defend it. And while the black king babysits the pawn, your king, which is far away, gains the tempi it was missing.
step.behind: Rook behind the pawn, then the king on its way.
step.behind.hint: Rc8, behind the pawn. Then the king comes: Ka7.
step.behind.done: Rook behind the pawn and king on its way. The black king has become the pawn's nanny, and your king will arrive before the pawn queens.
step.race: Now there is no cut and no shortcut: you count. The pawn needs three moves to reach f1. Your king has to arrive in time to help the rook win the pawn. The shortest way is diagonal, towards the squares in front of the pawn. Lose one move and the sums no longer add up.
step.count: Count and run. Your king has exactly the moves it needs, not one more.
step.count.hint: Kc6, Kd5 and Kd4: always diagonally, towards the pawn.
step.count.done: Just in time. The white king stands next to the squares the pawn has to cross, the rook goes to the f-file, and the pawn falls. Notice that any other first move would already have drawn.
step.late: The same position with your king one square further away. Now the sums do not add up: whichever way it goes, your king arrives one move later than needed, and the black king escorts the pawn to the end. It is a draw. In this ending a single tempo decides everything. That is why you count before you play.
step.bodycheck: When both kings race to the same place, push with your shoulder. The black king wants to reach d3 and d2, next to the pawn. Your king can step into its way: it takes the squares the black king needs, and the black king is left outside, far from the pawn. That is the shoulder: your king pushes the other one away without touching it.
step.shoulder: Put your king in the black king's way and stay there.
step.shoulder.hint: Kd5, attacking the pawn. After c3, Kc4, which takes d3 from the black king. After c2, Kc3.
step.shoulder.done: The black king never got near the pawn. Your king stood between them, and the rook finishes the job.
step.block: The shoulder works for both sides. Here it is the black king that blocks the way: on e5 it rules out d6 and e6, and your king cannot go through there. Do not force it. Walk around by the c-file, in front of the pawn, and use the rook to hold the pawn from behind.
step.around: Go around the black king, hold the pawn with the rook and arrive in front.
step.around.hint: Kc6, going around the black king. Then Rd1 behind the pawn, Kc5 and Kc4.
step.around.done: You went around the black king's shoulder and arrived in front of the pawn. With the rook behind and the king in front, the pawn has nowhere to go.
step.tempo: Sometimes the black king stands on the perfect square, in front of the pawn, and your king cannot arrive in time. That is when the tempo-gaining check comes in. The rook checks and forces the black king to pick a side. Whichever it picks, it leaves the front of the pawn, and that one move is exactly what your king needed. This example comes from Ezryn's study on Lichess.
step.check: Give the tempo-gaining check and bring the rook back behind the pawn.
step.check.hint: Re8+. After Kf3, the rook goes back behind the pawn: Rd8.
step.check.done: The check moved the black king away from the front of the pawn. Now it needs a move to come back, and in that move your king walks around and arrives.
step.t_knight: The white king has arrived and the rook threatens mate. It looks lost for Black. Does Black have any resource that saves the game?
step.t_knight.hint1: Promoting to a queen loses. Think of a promotion that comes with check.
step.knight: Now the other side. Black has lost the count: the white king has arrived and the rook threatens mate on a1. Promoting to a queen loses at once: Ra1 is mate. But there is e1=N+, checking the white king. The knight sticks to its own king, the rook cannot separate them, and it is a draw. Whoever defends with the pawn has to know this resource; whoever has the rook has to avoid falling for it.
step.rush: This is how you fall into the trap. White had a winning position and rushed the king to e3. The black king went to e1, and Rh8 seemed to win, threatening mate on h1. But then came d1=N+, with check, and the knight saved everything. The hurry took the king to e3, exactly a square where the newborn knight gives check.
step.trap: The same position, before the mistake. Win without giving the knight a chance.
step.trap.hint: Do not move the king yet. Rd8, behind the pawn. After the black king goes to c2, Ke2 and Rxd2.
step.trap.done: The rook attacked the pawn from behind and the white king arrived via e2, where no knight check gains anything. First the rook, then the king.
step.t_saavedra: Now the pawn is yours, against the rook. It is two steps from promoting, but the rook keeps harassing. How does the pawn win?
step.t_saavedra.hint1: Watch out for stalemate after the promotion. Not every promotion has to be a queen.
step.saavedra: A curiosity to finish. As a rule, pawn against rook is the pawn fighting for a draw. But there is the Saavedra position, from 1895, in which the pawn wins. After c7 and a series of checks, Black sets up a stalemate: if the pawn becomes a queen, the rook offers itself and no move is left. Saavedra found the answer: promote to a rook. No stalemate, and a mating threat. The knight promotion you saw today is a cousin of that idea: sometimes the smaller piece is worth more.
step.recap: Three rules. One: first of all, cut the king off with the rook, or put the rook behind the pawn. Two: count the tempi; your king walks diagonally, and if the black king blocks the way, use your shoulder or go around in front of the pawn. Three: beware of the knight; do not take your king to a square where the promotion gives check.
step.finish: Now you play, against the machine. Cut off the black king or put the rook behind the pawn, count the tempi and beware of the knight.
ex.e01: White to play and win. The black king wants to come down and escort the pawn. Do not let it.
ex.e01.hint: The rook can draw a line the black king cannot cross.
ex.e01.solution: Ra5. The rook cuts the black king off on the fifth rank and the pawn is left alone: if it advances, the rook goes after it. The other moves let the black king reach the pawn, and then your king, far away, does not come back in time.
ex.e02: White to play and win. The kings face each other. Where does the rook work best?
ex.e02.hint: The pawn should only move with its king beside it.
ex.e02.solution: Rd1. With the rook behind the pawn, it cannot advance without protection, and the black king is tied to it. Your king walks around and arrives. It is the only winning move.
ex.e03: White to play and win. It is a race: your king is far away. What is the first step?
ex.e03.hint: Count the squares. Which is the shortest way to the front of the pawn?
ex.e03.solution: Kb6, diagonally, heading for c5 and c4. Any other king move arrives one tempo late, and a rook move now does not change the count: the black king escorts the pawn and it is a draw.
ex.e04: White to play and win. The black king stands in front of the pawn, on the ideal square. How do you get it out of there?
ex.e04.hint: A check that forces the king to pick a side.
ex.e04.solution: Rd8+. The black king leaves the front of the pawn; after Ke3, Rc8 attacks the pawn from behind and it needs an escort (Kd6 also wins). That gained tempo is what your king needed to walk around. It is a position from Ezryn's study, one file to the side.
ex.e05: White to play and win. The black king wants to get next to the pawn. Use your shoulder.
ex.e05.hint: Your king can take the squares the black king would walk through.
ex.e05.solution: Ke5, which takes e4 from the black king; after f3, Kf4, which takes e3. The black king is left outside, and after f2, Kf3 and the rook win the pawn.
ex.e06: White to play and draw. You have the pawn; Black has the rook. Promoting to a queen looks natural. Look first.
ex.e06.hint: After the promotion, the black rook has a check on the eighth rank. Which piece would prevent that?
ex.e06.solution: f8=N+. With check, the knight gains the tempo that was missing and sticks to its king. f8=Q loses at once: Ra8 is mate, because the black king on e6 covers d7, e7 and f7. Moving the king loses too.
ex.e07: Black to play and draw. You have the pawn, and the white king is coming for it. Where does your king go?
ex.e07.hint: The pawn's king has to walk in front of it, not behind it.
ex.e07.solution: Kf3, heading for e2, in front of the pawn. Moves like Kf4 or Kf5 leave the king beside or behind the pawn, and the white king arrives in time. With the king in front, the pawn advances protected and the rook cannot win it.
ex.e08: White to play and win. The pawn is one step from queening and your king is close. Beware of haste.
ex.e08.hint: Think about what happens if the white king gets close to the pawn and Black promotes to a knight.
ex.e08.solution: Re8, behind the pawn, and only then the king, via f2. Any rook move along the eighth rank also wins. Moving the king first draws: after Kf3 Kf1 and Rh8 comes e1=N+, with check. It is a chapter of Kyrylo27's study on Lichess.
ex.e09: White to play and win. The black king blocks the direct route. Find the detour and do not waste time.
ex.e09.hint: Go around on the pawn's side and, when the black king leans on the pawn, pin the pawn down from behind.
ex.e09.solution: Kd7, heading for the c-file; after Kd5, Rc1 behind the pawn; after Kc5, Kc7, keeping the black king busy. Each of these moves is the only one that wins. Going in a straight line runs into the black king's shoulder.
ex.e10: White to play and win. The rook is already in place. Bring the king to the pawn without giving the black king a chance.
ex.e10.hint: First, a king move that takes the central squares from the black king. Then diagonally, in front of the pawn.
ex.e10.solution: Ke6, the only winning move: the king takes d5 and e5. After Ke4, Kd6 (Re1+ also works); after Ke3, Kc5 or Kd5, and the king reaches c4 in front of the pawn. Race, shoulder and counting in one exercise.
key.cut: The cut-off: Ra5 separates the black king from the pawn. Own position, checked in the tablebase.
key.shoulder: The shoulder: Kd5 and Kc4 take the squares next to the pawn from the black king. Own position, checked in the tablebase.
key.check: The tempo-gaining check: Re8+. From Ezryn's study "Principles of Rook vs Pawn Endgame" on Lichess.
key.knight: The knight defence: e1=N+ draws, e1=Q loses. From Kyrylo27's study "Rook versus Pawn" on Lichess.
key.saavedra: The Saavedra position (1895): the pawn beats the rook by promoting to a rook. As shown on Wikipedia.
history: Rook against pawn is one of the oldest endings in the manuals, and its most famous case is an exception. In 1875, in a game between Fenton and Potter, a rook-against-pawn position arose that ended in a draw. Twenty years later, in 1895, G. E. Barbier published a version of it in the Glasgow Weekly Citizen as a draw. Fernando Saavedra, a Spanish priest living in the city, showed that White won by promoting the pawn to a rook, not a queen, to avoid stalemate. Lasker gave the position the form known today. Exceptions aside, the practical rule is the one in this lesson: with the king far away, the rook draws against an advanced pawn; with the king close, it wins. The tablebase decides each case, often by a single tempo.
practice: Now against the machine: rook against pawn, and your king is far away. Count the tempi, walk diagonally and give the knight no chance. The goal is to win.
